paper_title: Harness-Model Collaboration for Long-Horizon Continual Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-horizon agents continuously encounter reusable procedural knowledge, yet existing systems typically rely either on model adaptation or external memory, trading persistent learning for rapid reuse. This limitation is especially important for Web agents that repeatedly execute related multi-step workflows. We propose HaMo, a Harness-Model collaborative framework that combines fast non-parametric experience accumulation with slow parametric adaptation. HaMo distills trajectories into strategy-level experience cards for immediate retrieval, while an experience-conditioned continual learning objective trains the model to interpret, ground, and execute retrieved strategies across changing contexts. A retrieval-coverage-based selection mechanism further identifies compact and complementary trajectories for parameter updates. Experiments show that HaMo outperforms harness-only and model-only adaptation under within-domain and cross-domain shifts, improving both retention and adaptation. These results highlight the importance of jointly preserving procedural experience and internalizing the competence to transfer and execute it across tasks.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
An agent that completes a long-horizon task today should be-
come better at solving related tasks tomorrow. Long-horizon
interactions naturally produce reusable procedural knowl-
edge [13, 36], yet agents without explicit cross-task learning
mechanisms treat each task as an isolated episode and cannot
systematically accumulate such experience over time. This
limitation is particularly important for Web agents, which
repeatedly perform multi-step workflows such as informa-
tion seeking, product search, and transactional tasks [3, 5, 8],
where knowledge acquired from previous interactions could
directly benefit future ones.
sections.content: A natural solution is model-level adaptation, where trajectories from previous tasks are used to update model parameters [2, 16, 29]. Such updates can turn past interactions into persistent behavioral competence, but frequent adaptation is costly and may interfere with previously acquired capabilities, especially under sequential distribution shifts [12, 26]. An alternative is harness-level adaptation, where useful experience is stored externally and retrieved Figure 1. Motivation for our method in continual learning for long-horizon agents. Harnessand model-only methods either enable fast experience reuse but tend to plateau, or suffer from instability and forgetting. HaMo combines both mechanisms to achieve steady improvement within domains and better retention across domain shifts. for future tasks [15, 37]. This enables newly acquired knowledge to affect behavior immediately without retraining, but the model itself does not necessarily become better at interpreting and executing the retrieved experience. Neither mechanism alone fully addresses continual learning in longhorizon agents (shown in Figure 1). We argue that these two forms of adaptation are naturally complementary because they operate at different timescales. strategy discovered from single trajectory may already be useful for future tasks, while still being too specific to justify an immediate parameter update. Such knowledge can first be stored externally and reused when similar situations arise. As related strategies recur across tasks, they provide stronger supervision for improving the model itself. For longhorizon agents, this process is not simply about memorizing past solutions: the key challenge is to internalize procedural competence, i.e., the ability to interpret high-level strategies, ground them in changing environments, and translate them into appropriate actions. Motivated by this observation, we propose HaMo, Harness-Model collaborative framework for continual learning in long-horizon agents. Our method separates adaptation into two tightly coupled processes. At the harness level, each trajectory is distilled into compact experience card containing the task context, initial conditions, and strategy-level solution outline. These cards are stored in persistent non-parametric memory, making newly acquired procedural knowledge immediately available to future tasks. At the model level, HaMo continually updates single parameter-efficient adapter using selected trajectories together with historical replay, improving the models ability to exploit accumulated experience while preserving previously acquired capabilities. key design of HaMo is experience-conditioned adaptation. Instead of learning only direct mapping from interaction context to action, the model is additionally conditioned on strategy-level experience retrieved from the harness. It therefore learns how to interpret and instantiate retrieved strategy under different observations, objects, states, and interaction histories. The same interface is used during inference: the harness retrieves relevant experience, while the adapted model determines how that experience should be executed in the current environment. In this way, the harness preserves reusable procedural knowledge, whereas model adaptation progressively internalizes the competence required to transfer and execute that knowledge across tasks. HaMo further addresses the redundancy of continual supervision. Although storing experience externally is inexpensive, repeatedly training on every observed trajectory is unnecessary because many trajectories encode similar strategies. We therefore introduce retrieval-coverage-based selection mechanism that identifies compact set of representative and complementary trajectories for parameter adaptation. An experience is preferred when it can support many other tasks through retrieval, while the selected set is encouraged to cover distinct strategy contexts. This concentrates parameter updates on broadly reusable procedural knowledge without requiring all stored trajectories to participate in training. We evaluate HaMo on continual streams of long-horizon tasks across ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, and WebShop, covering both within-domain and cross-domain settings. WebShop provides an interactive Web-agent environment, while the other benchmarks test whether the proposed learning mechanism generalizes beyond single domain. The results show clear complementarity between harnessand model-level adaptation: harness-only learning enables rapid reuse of experience but reaches performance ceiling, whereas modelonly adaptation can acquire strong task-specific capabilities but suffers substantial forgetting under distribution shifts. HaMo combines the strengths of both, achieving stronger continual adaptation while better retaining previously acquired capabilities.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
2.1 LLMs for Long-Horizon Tasks
sections.content: Long-horizon agents must sustain goal-directed behavior over extended, failure-prone trajectories [4]. Prior work improves reasoning, planning, and web interaction through Bi et al. reasoning-action interleaving [31], stateful benchmarks [40], system-level analyses [14], search and reflection [39], action knowledge [41], global planning [20], and curriculum-based reinforcement learning [9, 10]. Complementary work improves experience reuse via trajectory compression [32], rollout aggregation [11], global memory [17], reusable workflows [28], and conditional memory [1]. We focus instead on retaining and consolidating reusable experience across continual long-horizon task streams. 2.2 Continual Learning for LLM Agents External-memory methods retain verbal feedback, skills, workflows, or structured memories without frequent weight updates [7, 18, 24, 28, 34, 38]. Parameter-based continual learning instead mitigates forgetting through parameter protection, replay [22], continual policy adaptation [25], or multiple retention anchors [35]. However, neither line directly decides which experience should remain externally retrievable and which should drive parameter updates. EvolvingAgent [6] combines evolving experience with continual world-model learning, while Dong et al. [4] highlight the broader connection between external experience and internalized competence. HaMo coordinates these two timescales: rapidly updated strategy-level memory supports immediate reuse, while selected trajectories and replay enable less frequent parameter adaptation.

sections.title:
3 Method
HaMo coordinates continual learning through two comple-
mentary mechanisms operating at different levels: a persis-
tent external memory at the harness level and continual
parameter adaptation at the model level. The harness re-
tains reusable strategy-level experience and makes newly
acquired knowledge immediately accessible without requir-
ing parameter updates. The model, in turn, is continually
adapted to interpret retrieved experience, ground it in the
current interaction context, and translate it into appropriate
actions. Training and inference share the same initial dia-
logue format: the user request, the initial observation, and
injected matched experience.

sections.title:
4 Experimental Setting
4.1 Datasets and Continual Learning Protocol
sections.content: We evaluate HaMo on three interactive benchmarks using their purely text-based environments. ScienceWorld [27] evaluates scientific reasoning through tasks that require agents to navigate an environment, manipulate objects, and carry out experiments. ALFWorld [19] provides household tasks in text environment aligned with embodied tasks, requiring agents to locate objects and perform operations such as moving, cleaning, heating, and cooling. WebShop [30] evaluates instruction-conditioned online shopping: agents search for products, inspect their descriptions, select options, and make purchases that satisfy user requirements. Together, these benchmarks cover scientific experimentation, household manipulation, and web-based decision making, with different action spaces and task semantics. We consider two continual learning settings. In withindomain continual learning, we divide the ScienceWorld training set into four equally sized subsets that are disjoint at the sample level. Every subset covers all task types, so the task-type coverage remains unchanged across stages even though the training samples are different. We introduce one subset at each successive stage, simulating within-domain data-incremental continual learning over fixed set of task types rather than the sequential introduction of new task types. After every stage, we evaluate the agent on the entire ScienceWorld test set, using the same evaluation set throughout the stream. In cross-domain continual learning, the agent learns sequentially on ScienceWorld (S), ALFWorld (A), and WebShop (W). After each stage, we evaluate all domains encountered so far, allowing us to examine both adaptation to the current domain and retention of earlier capabilities. The main cross-domain experiment uses the order W; the order ablation additionally considers and A. 4.2 Baselines We use Qwen3 [23] as the common backbone, evaluating Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B in the within-domain setting. Cross-domain experiments and component and trainingorder ablations use Qwen3-8B, while the model-scale ablation additionally evaluates Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B. Thinking mode is disabled for all Qwen3 agents. Base denotes the backbone without the additional agent training or external harness considered here. Base+Harness augments the backbone with external experience while keeping its parameters fixed, isolating adaptation through the harness. We also compare two agent-training approaches instantiated on the Qwen3 backbone. AgentTuning [33] develops agent capabilities through instruction tuning on interaction trajectories; its original formulation mixes agent trajectories with general instruction data. ETO [21], or Exploration-Based Trajectory Optimization, uses exploration to collect failed trajectories and constructs trajectory preference pairs for policy optimization. These comparisons evaluate how agenttraining approaches behave under our continual learning settings. HaMo combines persistent strategy memory, model adaptation conditioned on experience, and historical replay, as described in Section 3. Its model updates use single continually updated LoRA adapter with frozen backbone. In the component ablation, Harness only corresponds to Base+Harness, while Model only performs sequential parameter adaptation without either the external harness or historical replay. This comparison examines the contribution of coordinating external experience with model adaptation. Implementation settings and framework pseudocode are provided in Appendices and B, respectively. 4.3 Metrics We use the native scoring mechanism of each text environment as the performance metric. For ScienceWorld, we report the environments task-progress score, which credits intermediate progress toward completing the scientific task. For ALFWorld, we report the task-completion score, averaged across episodes as success rate. For WebShop, we report the environment reward measuring how well the purchased product satisfies the requested specifications, retaining partial credit rather than reducing the outcome to binary success. Scores are presented on 0100 scale, with higher values indicating better performance. Each evaluation episode is limited to 50 agentenvironment interaction turns and ends earlier if the environment terminates the task. For the within-domain experiment, Average summarizes the four reported stage scores; the Base score gives the fixed backbone reference. In the cross-domain performance plots, each panel corresponds to completed training stage and shows scores on the evaluated domains. We assess retention by comparing domains score immediately after learning it with its scores after subsequent stages. The training-order ablation also reports the sum of the three final-domain scores as descriptive aggregate. Since the benchmarks use different scoring semantics, this sum complements the per-domain results rather than representing pooled task-success rate. Bi et al. Bar groups compare methods, and colors indicate evaluation domains. Higher scores are better. 5 Results 5.1 Main Results 5.1.1 Within-Domain Continual Learning. Figure 3 shows that HaMo improves on the full ScienceWorld test set as additional training subsets arrive, for both model sizes. With Qwen3-8B, its score increases from 38.13 to 60.49, yielding four-stage average of 52.22. With Qwen3-14B, it increases from 38.61 to 61.15, with an average of 53.09. These averages exceed Base+Harness by 13.88 and 12.44 points, respectively, using the reported values. The final-stage gains over the unadapted backbones are 22.94 points for 8B and 21.20 points for 14B. 5.1.2 Cross-Domain Continual Learning. Figure 4 evaluates the stream. After the final stage, HaMo obtains 52.43 on ScienceWorld, 66.79 on ALFWorld, and 59.64 on WebShop, outperforming every listed baseline on each domain. Relative to Base, these are gains of 14.88, 22.26, and 13.96 points. Relative to the strongest non-HaMo baseline for each final-domain score, the gains are 13.02 points on ScienceWorld, 19.71 on ALFWorld, and 5.16 on WebShop. stage averages alone do not isolate retention of individual task types. The advantage emerges over successive stages rather than from uniformly stronger initial performance. At Stage 1, HaMo scores slightly below Base+Harness for both backbones, but it leads all listed methods from Stage 2 onward. Base+Harness remains close to the backbone reference throughout the stream, suggesting that external experience alone provides limited improvement in this setting. AgentTuning and ETO exhibit different trajectories across model sizes: their 8B scores decline overall, whereas their 14B scores recover after low first stage. Nevertheless, their four-stage averages remain below those of HaMo. These results support the value of jointly adapting the model and its experience context for sustained improvement within ScienceWorld; the The intermediate evaluations reveal how these gains arise. HaMo scores 52.43 on ScienceWorld after the first stage, improves to 54.19 after learning ALFWorld, and returns to 52.43 after learning WebShop. Thus, its final ScienceWorld score matches its score immediately after ScienceWorld training, although it is 1.76 points below the intermediate peak. Its ALFWorld score decreases moderately from 70.08 to 66.79 after WebShop training. In contrast, AgentTunings ScienceWorld score falls from 26.24 to 3.13, and ETOs falls from 20.16 to 3.20. Both methods improve over Base on the final WebShop task but finish below Base on the two earlier domains. Under this protocol, successful adaptation to the latest domain therefore does not ensure retention of earlier capabilities. HarnessModel Collaboration for Long-Horizon Continual Learning Figure 5. Final-stage total (S+A+W) sums the three dataset scores measured after the final training stage for each training order. Base+Harness largely preserves the backbones earlierdomain performance, but its final WebShop score of 43.42 is below the Base score of 45.68. HaMo combines stronger acquisition of new-domain capabilities with substantially better earlier-domain performance than the trajectory-training baselines. This pattern is consistent with the intended complementarity of persistent strategy access and continual learning of how to execute those strategies. 5.2 Ablation Results 5.2.1 HarnessModel Collaboration. Figure 5 compares HaMo with harness-only and model-only adaptation. Harness only provides relatively small changes from Base, whereas Model only substantially improves newly learned tasks: it obtains 53.98 on ScienceWorld after the first stage and 73.72 on ALFWorld after the second. However, its ScienceWorld score drops to 22.18 after ALFWorld training and finishes at 24.57, decline of 29.41 points from its first-stage score. HaMo instead finishes at 52.43 on ScienceWorld, exceeding Model only by 27.86 points and matching its own first-stage score. This retention benefit comes with measurable tradeoff. Model only achieves higher final ALFWorld score than HaMo (69.34 versus 66.79), while HaMo is slightly better on WebShop (59.64 versus 58.74). HaMo therefore does not dominate parameter-only adaptation on every domain. Figure 8 evaluates HaMo with Qwen3 models of different scales, including 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters. HaMo remains effective across all three model sizes throughout the continual learning stream, indicating that its benefit is not restricted to particular model capacity. Larger LLMs generally show stronger acquisition of newly introduced tasks, especially after adapting to later domains, suggesting that increased model capacity provides greater flexibility for incorporating new procedural knowledge. 5.2.4 Case Study: Experience-Guided Constraint Verification. Table 1 illustrates experience-guided constraint verification. The task requires caramel-flavored, chocolatecoated wafers in 4.41-ounce size below $60. Base purchases hazelnut product without resolving the flavor mismatch, scoring 25. HaMo recognizes that the candidates Triple Dark title does not establish caramel match and checks the available options, scoring 100. This follows the retrieved cards instruction to recheck requirements against the current task; HaMo also checks the current $60 budget rather than the references $70 limit. The actions click[caramel] and click[4.41 ounce] produce neither visible observation change nor an immediate reward. They indicate attempted grounding of the requested attributes, but do not establish state changes or causally explain the reward gain. sections.title:
6 Conclusion
We presented HaMo, a harness–model collaborative frame-
work for continual learning in long-horizon agents. HaMo
combines persistent strategy-level memory with experience-
conditioned parameter adaptation, enabling newly acquired
procedural knowledge to be reused immediately while grad-
ually improving the model’s ability to interpret and exe-
cute retrieved strategies. Experiments on ScienceWorld, ALF-
World, and WebShop show that HaMo achieves a better bal-
ance between adaptation and retention than harness-only
or model-only approaches, with stronger robustness under
both within-domain and cross-domain continual learning.
These results highlight the value of coordinating external
experience accumulation with internal model adaptation,
and suggest a promising direction for building long-horizon
agents that can continually learn from interaction while
preserving previously acquired capabilities.
sections.content: Limitations HaMo can offset part of the forgetting induced by crossdomain training, but it does not fully prevent catastrophic forgetting. Subsequent adaptation may still reduce performance on previously learned domains, and the degree of retention depends on the domain sequence. The current results therefore support partial mitigation of forgetting rather than complete immunity to it.

sections.title: Future Work
sections.content: Adaptive experience use. useful extension is to learn when to retrieve strategy, when to reject an unsuitable card, and when to refresh guidance during execution. Such decisions could combine retrieval confidence with observed task progress and explicit checks of strategy preconditions. This would allow the agent to respond to misleading experience rather than treating retrieval similarity as sufficient evidence of applicability. Stronger evaluation and broader environments. Controlled ablations of replay, anchor selection, experience conditioning, and decoding temperature would clarify their individual contributions and interactions. Repeated runs and longer task streams could assess variability and persistent forgetting, while end-to-end cost measurements would expose the tradeoff between performance and memory maintenance. Extending the framework to multimodal agents and changing web environments would further test whether experience-conditioned execution transfers beyond the present text-based benchmarks. sections.title: Settings
sections.content: Experiments use NVIDIA A800 GPUs with 80 GB device memory. At each adaptation stage, we train the selected anchor trajectories together with historical replay for three epochs at learning rate of 2 104. Only the LoRA adapter is updated, with rank 𝑟 = 16 and scaling parameter 𝛼 = 32; the backbone remains frozen. The same adapter is carried forward across stages rather than reinitialized or replaced by task-specific adapter. Table 2 summarizes the settings. Table 2. HaMo implementation and evaluation settings. Setting Value GPU hardware Training epochs per stage Learning rate LoRA rank 𝑟 LoRA scaling parameter 𝛼 Backbone parameters Adapter management Inference temperature Maximum interaction turns Coverage-selection neighbors Anchor budget Memory release NVIDIA A800, 80 GB 3 2 104 16 32 Frozen One adapter, updated sequentially 0.7 50 per episode 3, excluding the query card Stage-specific coverage-curve knee Disabled; all cards retained Stochastic agent inference. We set the inference temperature to 0.7 to retain diversity in action generation after trajectory-based training. Interactive tasks may require the agent to adjust its decisions when the current state differs from retrieved example; sampling is intended to reduce overly deterministic execution patterns and allow alternative actions. This is decoding choice, not training regularizer or guarantee against overfitting. We do not attribute the reported gains specifically to temperature, since temperature ablation is not included. Bi et al. Evaluation protocol. Each episode ends when the environment terminates or after 50 interaction turns. We use the native task scores and report them on 0100 scale, retaining partial credit for ScienceWorld and WebShop. The within-domain protocol uses four sample-disjoint ScienceWorld training stages and evaluates the full test set after each stage. Cross-domain evaluation follows the task orders described in Section 4 and measures performance on domains encountered so far.
